provisioning:Cours Lafayette.name: Cours Lafayette market
provisioning:Cours Lafayette.teaser: A kilometre of fish, cheese and growers' crates, Tuesday to Sunday, packed away by half past twelve
provisioning:Cours Lafayette.story: For a cook this is Toulon's daily shop. Work the cours from the Place Louis Blanc end: the fishmongers first, while the ice is fresh, then the cheesemongers, the charcuterie and the Provençal growers with the week's vegetables. Buy the fish early and keep it cold, and leave the heavy produce for last so you carry less. The cade carts at that end have their own card.
provisioning:Cours Lafayette.why: Shop before ten for the fish; the food stalls pack up around half past twelve and only non-food stalls stay on.
facts: The day's fish, a local cheese, charcuterie and seasonal vegetables from the growers' stalls
Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 7.30am to 12.30pm; closed Monday (seen Jul 2026)

provisioning:Sanary's Wednesday market.name: Sanary Wednesday market
provisioning:Sanary's Wednesday market.teaser: Wednesday on the port at Sanary: the big market under the plane trees, the fishing boats a few steps away
provisioning:Sanary's Wednesday market.story: Every Wednesday morning the stalls run along the port of Sanary-sur-Mer, under the plane trees of the Allées d'Estienne d'Orves, from about 8am until 1pm: tomatoes, tapenade, cade and chickpea galettes, cheese, flowers and the rest of a Provençal larder. In 2018 TF1 viewers voted it France's most beautiful market, a public vote for looks rather than a food award, and the crowds followed. The better buy is often separate: on Quai Charles de Gaulle the town's fishermen sell the morning catch straight off their little pointus, when the sea allows.
provisioning:Sanary's Wednesday market.why: Arrive by nine, before the aisles fill, and look at the fishermen's stalls on the quay before anything else.
facts: Wednesday; smaller morning markets run on other days
About 8am to 1pm (seen Jul 2026; no 2026 schedule found online)
The fishermen's stalls on Quai Charles de Gaulle: daurade, denti or merlan when the boats have been out; no fixed days, and nothing after a rough sea

provisioning:The Aups truffle market.name: Aups truffle market
provisioning:The Aups truffle market.teaser: Thursday mornings in winter, Place Mistral in Aups trades black truffles until the baskets are empty
provisioning:The Aups truffle market.story: From late November the Haut-Var's truffle hunters bring the black winter truffle, Tuber melanosporum, to Place Frédéric Mistral in Aups every Thursday morning. The 2026-27 season opens on Thursday 26 November 2026 with a ceremony at 9am and is listed to run until 25 March 2027, though a poor year cuts it short, and selling stops once the truffles are gone, often well before noon. Smell before you buy. In January the town holds its Fête de la Truffe, with dog-and-handler hunting demonstrations, a producers' market and a charity truffle auction.
provisioning:The Aups truffle market.why: Be on the square at 9am on a January Thursday, when the old calendar puts the truffle at full strength.
facts: 9am to noon, or until sold out (Oct 2026)
Black winter truffles with a strong smell; the Fête de la Truffe in January (held on 25 January in 2026; the 2027 date was not yet listed in October)

provisioning:Vieux Moulin du Partégal.name: Vieux Moulin du Partégal
provisioning:Vieux Moulin du Partégal.teaser: A 16th-century olive mill east of Toulon where the guided tour and the tasting cost nothing
provisioning:Vieux Moulin du Partégal.story: The Vieux Moulin à huile du Partégal stands on the chemin des Laures at La Farlède, in the valley east of Toulon, and dates from the 16th century. The guided visit, in French or English, takes about an hour and a quarter: the old mill, how the olives become oil, then the tasting table, where several oils are poured side by side before tapenades and other local products. For a cook stocking a galley, it is the simplest way to taste Provençal oils against each other before choosing which bottles to buy.
provisioning:Vieux Moulin du Partégal.why: Book the English tour (9.30am or 2.30pm) and buy the oil at the end, once you know which one you like.
facts: Monday to Saturday, closed Sunday; tours roughly on the hour April to September, by booking outside that (Oct 2026; hours differ between listings, check)
Olive oil, tapenade and local products
Tour and tasting free for individuals; groups of 15 to 25 pay €4 per adult (Oct 2026)

provisioning:The Solliès fig growers.name: Solliès fig growers
provisioning:The Solliès fig growers.teaser: France's only AOP fig, bought from the Gapeau valley growers from mid-August into October
provisioning:The Solliès fig growers.story: The Figue de Solliès is the violet-black Bourjassotte Noire, grown in the Gapeau valley around Solliès-Pont, east of Toulon. The harvest opens around 15 August, a second crop follows in September, and the last fruit comes in October, so mid-autumn is the tail of the season. Buy from village stalls and markets, where growers sell trays picked that morning: soft, heavy figs that should give slightly under the thumb. At the end of August the fig fair fills the centre of Solliès-Pont; its 29th edition, on 29 and 30 August 2026, drew about 150 exhibitors.
provisioning:The Solliès fig growers.why: Eat one at the stall and buy only what you will use within a day or two; ripe figs do not travel.
facts: Village stalls and markets around Solliès-Pont, in the Gapeau valley
Mid-August into October; the fig fair is the last weekend of August (29-30 Aug in 2026, free entry)
Fresh AOP Figue de Solliès by the tray; the fig liqueur, Fleur de Figue, has its own card

provisioning:Confiserie Azuréenne.name: Confiserie Azuréenne
provisioning:Confiserie Azuréenne.teaser: October in Collobrières: crème de marrons by the jar for the galley, a few marrons glacés for the table
provisioning:Confiserie Azuréenne.story: This is where to stock the chestnut shelf. Buy crème de marrons by the jar, to spoon over yoghurt or a crêpe, loose marrons glacés to serve at the end of a dinner, and the chestnut alcohol for a digestif. The village boutique is on Boulevard Kœnig, facing the Pont Vieux. October, when the new chestnuts arrive, is the month to come.
provisioning:Confiserie Azuréenne.why: Buy the cream for cooking and the glacés for the table; the cream is the one you will use.
facts: Crème de marrons, marrons glacés, chestnut liqueur
Any time; October for the new season, but avoid the festival Sundays (18 and 25 Oct 2026) if you need to park

provisioning:Maison des Vins de Bandol.name: Maison des Vins de Bandol
provisioning:Maison des Vins de Bandol.teaser: The appellation's own cellar below Le Castellet: Bandol reds and rosés side by side, with advisers to help
provisioning:Maison des Vins de Bandol.story: Despite the name, it is not in Bandol. The appellation's tasting cellar sits among the vines at the entrance to Le Castellet, on the chemin de la Ferrage. Bandol covers eight communes, from Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer and La Cadière-d'Azur to Le Beausset, Évenos and Ollioules, and this is the easy place to taste across them: Mourvèdre reds next to rosés, with advisers behind the counter who will help you choose cases for the boat. In Bandol town, the separate Oenothèque on Place Lucien Artaud also sells the appellation and receives growers mainly in July and August.
provisioning:Maison des Vins de Bandol.why: Taste the reds here first, then drive up to the estates you liked; Tempier and Pibarnon have their own cards.
facts: 238 chemin de la Ferrage, at the entrance to Le Castellet
All year, Tuesday to Saturday, 10am-1pm and 3pm-6pm (to 7pm in summer); closed Sunday and Monday (Oct 2026, tourist-office listing)
Bandol red, rosé and white from across the appellation

provisioning:Maison des Vins Côtes de Pr.name: Maison des Vins Côtes de Provence
provisioning:Maison des Vins Côtes de Pr.teaser: More than 800 Côtes de Provence wines under one roof on the old RN7, at the prices the estates charge
provisioning:Maison des Vins Côtes de Pr.story: Founded in 1986 on the old Nationale 7 at Les Arcs-sur-Argens, between Vidauban and Draguignan, this is the appellation's shop window: more than 800 Côtes de Provence wines, sold at producer prices. It saves a day of driving between cellars when you need to fill a wine store for a charter, and it carries the reds and whites most visitors never meet alongside the rosé. From September to December 2026 the house oenologists run a three-hour morning class on set dates, six wines poured, for anyone who wants to learn the appellation before buying.
provisioning:Maison des Vins Côtes de Pr.why: Use it to taste across the appellation before you commit a morning to one estate.
facts: RN7, Les Arcs-sur-Argens, between Vidauban and Draguignan
Monday to Saturday, 10am-1pm and 2pm-6pm; closed Sunday (winter 2026 listing; summer hours may differ)
Côtes de Provence rosé, red and white from many estates

provisioning:Cave de la Capte.name: Cave de la Capte
provisioning:Cave de la Capte.teaser: On the Giens road since 1995: an organic-leaning bottle shop to fill the cooler on the way to the water
provisioning:Cave de la Capte.story: Hyères has no true natural-wine bar; that scene lives twenty minutes west in Toulon, and its rooms have their own cards. What Hyères does have is this caviste, opened in 1995 on the road out to the Giens peninsula: about 250 m² of shelves leaning towards organic, biodynamic and low-intervention bottles, with fine groceries alongside. It is a shop, not a bar, so buy here and drink somewhere else. Sitting between the town and La Capte, it makes an easy stop on the way to the peninsula's walks or the island boats.
provisioning:Cave de la Capte.why: Ask for Var growers who farm organically and take a few bottles for a Giens or island picnic.
facts: Monday to Saturday 9.30am-12.30pm and 3.45pm-7.15pm, Sunday morning (2021 listing, the latest found; check)

walks:Presqu'île de Giens & the salt pan.name: Presqu'île de Giens
walks:Presqu'île de Giens & the salt pan.teaser: Two sand bars tie Giens to the mainland, with flamingos standing in the old salt pans between them
walks:Presqu'île de Giens & the salt pan.story: Giens is an island that got caught. Two parallel sand bars, a rare double tombolo, fasten it to the coast at Hyères and enclose the old Salins des Pesquiers, where the Salins du Midi company made salt until 1995. The Conservatoire du littoral has owned the marsh since 2001, and pink flamingos stand in it all year, at their most numerous, around 2,000, in late summer. The path round the wild west and south shores follows the old customs patrols' beat, and a 1976 law keeps a three-metre strip along the French shore open to walkers, even across private land.
walks:Presqu'île de Giens & the salt pan.why: Walk the cliffs of the south shore with the wind in your face, then come back past the salt pans in the late light for the birds.
facts: Giens village, at the tip of the peninsula, for the coast path
Rocky coastal path, steep and wind-exposed in places
Late afternoon, for the flamingos on the pans

walks:The customs path, Gigaro to L'Esca.name: Gigaro to L'Escalet
walks:The customs path, Gigaro to L'Esca.teaser: The old customs path from La Croix-Valmer to Ramatuelle, cape by cape past Lardier and Taillat
walks:The customs path, Gigaro to L'Esca.story: Long before the beach clubs, men in uniform walked this shore watching for smugglers. The sentier du littoral is often dated to 1791, the year the revolutionary state founded its customs service, though no source pins down when this stretch was first cut. Today it threads the protected capes between Gigaro, at La Croix-Valmer, and L'Escalet in Ramatuelle: up over Cap Lardier through cistus and heather, down to coves of coarse sand, round past Cap Taillat, which has its own card, with the sea working at the rocks below.
walks:The customs path, Gigaro to L'Esca.why: Start early from Gigaro, swim at Cap Taillat at midday, and arrange a pick-up at L'Escalet so you do not have to walk back.
facts: Rocky coastal path with steep ups and downs through low maquis; little shade
A swim off the sand neck at Cap Taillat
Plenty of water, swim things, shoes with grip

walks:Mont Faron.name: Mont Faron
walks:Mont Faron.teaser: Six minutes by cable car above Toulon, and the whole roadstead lies at your feet
walks:Mont Faron.story: From the top of Mont Faron, 584 m above the town, the rade of Toulon is laid out whole: one of Europe's great natural roadsteads, the naval base with its grey hulls along the quays, ferries working in and out of the old port, and on a clear day the Massif de la Sainte-Baume on the skyline. The cable car climbs from Boulevard Amiral Vence in about six minutes. At the top, paths run along the limestone ridge between viewpoints, and a memorial to the August 1944 landings stands near the summit; its story is on its own card.
walks:Mont Faron.why: Go up on a clear morning, then come back down and see the same harbour from the water on a boat tour from Quai Cronstadt.
facts: Lower cable-car station, Boulevard Amiral Vence, Toulon
About 6 minutes up by cable car; it runs daily from early February to late November 2026, with technical closure days, and stops in high wind or on severe fire-risk days (Oct 2026)

walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.name: Sentier Blanc-Martel
walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.teaser: Sixteen kilometres down through the Verdon gorge, with steel ladders and a 670 m tunnel in the dark
walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.story: In August 1905 the speleologist Édouard-Alfred Martel, sent by the Ministry of Agriculture to look for drinking water for Provence, made the first full traverse of the Verdon gorge, guided by Isidore Blanc, the schoolmaster of Rougon. The Touring Club de France built the path between 1926 and 1928, ladders at the Brèche Imbert included, and Blanc worked on it until his accidental death in 1933; it has carried both names since 2005. It runs on the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence bank, down from the Chalet de la Maline to the river and out through unlit tunnels near the Couloir Samson.
walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.why: Take the shuttle and walk it one way; the long tunnel at the end, torch in hand, is the part you will remember.
facts: Chalet de la Maline, above La Palud-sur-Verdon. Morning shuttle from La Palud village to La Maline, afternoon return from the Point Sublime: weekends until about 1-2 November 2026, daily in high summer; book at navette.parcduverdon.fr (Oct 2026)
Steep descent, steel ladders, rocky riverside path and an unlit tunnel of about 670 m
Start on the first morning shuttle

walks:Up to the Chartreuse de la Verne.name: Chartreuse de la Verne
walks:Up to the Chartreuse de la Verne.teaser: A dark-stone monastery on a Maures ridge, founded around 1170 and silent again since 1983
walks:Up to the Chartreuse de la Verne.story: The Carthusians came to this ridge above the chestnut woods around 1170, under the bishops of Toulon and Fréjus, and their first church was consecrated on 3 October 1174. The lords of Bormes pillaged it in 1416; the Revolution confiscated it in 1789 and the monks left. The green-black serpentine framing its doorways was quarried nearby in the Maures. Listed as a historic monument since 1921, it has been home since 1983 to the nuns of the monastic Family of Bethlehem, so you visit the edges of a working silence, booklet in hand, with the forest close on every side.
walks:Up to the Chartreuse de la Verne.why: Leave the car at the end of the road, walk the last ten minutes in, and keep your voice down once inside the walls.
facts: Forest road from Collobrières to a free car park at the road's end, then about 10 minutes on a dirt track (Oct 2026)

calas:Plage Notre-Dame.name: Plage Notre-Dame
calas:Plage Notre-Dame.teaser: Eight hundred metres of pale sand under the pines, on the Porquerolles bay that turns its back to the mistral
calas:Plage Notre-Dame.story: On 22 February 1912 François-Joseph Fournier, who had made his fortune from a gold lode in Mexico, bought almost all of Porquerolles at auction as a present for his wife Sylvia, then planted the eucalyptus, mimosa and umbrella pines that still shade its tracks. The French state bought most of the island in 1971. Notre-Dame is the long bay east of the village, about 800 m of pale sand with Aleppo pines growing almost to the water, angled so it is sheltered from both the mistral and the east wind. European Best Destinations named it Europe's most beautiful beach in 2015.
calas:Plage Notre-Dame.why: Come in the shoulder months; in peak summer the island caps visitors at 6,000 a day, and the bay feels it.
facts: Boat to Porquerolles village (the islands card has the crossings), then about 30 minutes on foot or by hired bike

calas:The underwater trail at La Palud.name: Sentier sous-marin de la Palud
calas:The underwater trail at La Palud.teaser: France's first underwater trail, laid in 1979: six buoys, a mask and fins, and grouper that hold their ground
calas:The underwater trail at La Palud.story: Port-Cros is a national park at sea as well as on land (the islands card tells how it began), and this is where you read it underwater. A path from the harbour reaches the Plage de la Palud in 40 to 45 minutes; from the beach, a marked snorkel loop of about 40 minutes swims out past six buoys with explanation panels, in a few metres of water. Below you are posidonia meadows, wrasse and grouper that do not bolt, because nobody has speared fish here for more than sixty years. Laid in 1979, it was France's first underwater trail.
calas:The underwater trail at La Palud.why: Go on a calm day; when the mistral blows hard, swimming here is advised against.
facts: Boat to Port-Cros, then 40-45 minutes on foot to the Plage de la Palud

calas:Cap Taillat.name: Cap Taillat
calas:Cap Taillat.teaser: A sand neck ties a scrubby islet to the shore, with a swim on either side of it
calas:Cap Taillat.story: Cap Taillat came close to being a holiday village. In 1970 a company bought 27 hectares here for 400 Club Med bungalows and a marina; Ramatuelle's mayor called in the Conservatoire du littoral, which bought the cape in 1987. What survived is a sand isthmus joining a scrubby islet to the shore, with clear water on both flanks, and on the ridge above it the Dolmen de Briande, a Neolithic tomb excavated in 1935, the southernmost in the Var. The maquis looks young because it is: the fire of 24 July 2017 burned some 550 hectares across Taillat and Cap Lardier.
calas:Cap Taillat.why: Swim on whichever side of the tombolo is out of the wind that day.
facts: About 2.5 km on the coastal path through the maquis; the customs-path card covers the whole route from Gigaro

calas:Pampelonne, the public end.name: Pampelonne, the public sand
calas:Pampelonne, the public end.teaser: Four and a half kilometres of Ramatuelle sand, rebuilt so the beach comes before the clubs
calas:Pampelonne, the public end.story: Pampelonne runs about 4.5 km along the east side of the Ramatuelle peninsula, some 27 hectares of sand. For decades the clubs crept forward onto it. A State development plan, approved by decree in December 2015, cut the beach concessions from 27 to 23 and moved their buildings back against the foot of the dune, demountable and mostly taken down in winter; the beach was reworked from April 2019 and the dune rebuilt in 2020. The sand is public. Spread a towel on the open stretches towards the Bonne Terrasse end or Tahiti, and walk past the clubs, which have their own cards.
calas:Pampelonne, the public end.why: Come out of season: by mid-October most clubs have shut or come down, and the whole bay belongs to walkers.
facts: By road from Ramatuelle to the car parks behind the beach

avoid:Saint-Tropez in August.name: Saint-Tropez in August
avoid:Saint-Tropez in August.teaser: You picture Bardot's fishing port; August gives you traffic, a wall of yachts and a square you cannot cross
avoid:Saint-Tropez in August.story: The picture in your head is a fishing port. In August the roads in are jammed for hours, the old quay is walled with superyachts moored stern-to, the Place des Lices is too full to walk through, and the rosé is priced for the view. Nothing is wrong with the town; it is the wrong month. The same harbour at the end of September and into early October fills instead with classic yachts racing in Les Voiles de Saint-Tropez, the light is softer, and the summer crowd has gone home.
avoid:Saint-Tropez in August.why: Move the visit to late September, or arrive by boat for a morning and leave before lunch.
facts: Hours of traffic on the approach roads, a quay lined with superyachts, terraces priced for the view

avoid:Eating on the photogenic quay.name: Eating on the photogenic quay
avoid:Eating on the photogenic quay.teaser: Photo menus and a host waving you in: on the harbour front you pay for the view, not the plate
avoid:Eating on the photogenic quay.story: The harbour-front terraces in Saint-Tropez, Sainte-Maxime and Cavalaire are easy to spot: laminated menus with photographs, a host on the pavement beckoning, the best view in town. You pay for that view, not for what arrives on the plate. The cooking the Var is proud of usually sits a street or two back from the water, or twenty minutes inland, in Maures villages such as Collobrières, La Garde-Freinet and Gassin, and in the wine hamlets around Bandol and La Londe, where locals eat for about half the price.
avoid:Eating on the photogenic quay.why: Follow the AOP, not the awning: choose the table whose wine list names local estates.
facts: Photo menus, a host waving from the pavement, a sea view folded into the bill
Walk two streets back, or drive inland to Collobrières, La Garde-Freinet or Gassin; the guide's table cards were picked on exactly this test

avoid:Thinking the Var stops at the beac.name: Thinking the Var stops at the beach
avoid:Thinking the Var stops at the beac.teaser: Most visitors never leave the coastal strip, and miss the truffle oaks, the chestnut woods and the gorge
avoid:Thinking the Var stops at the beac.story: Most visitors never leave the strip along the sea, and so they miss the department's real larder: the truffle oaks of the Haut-Var, the chestnut woods of the Maures, and the Verdon gorge, cold water when the coast is roasting. Give the interior one whole day and time it to the calendar. This autumn that means Collobrières on a chestnut-festival Sunday; from late November, the Thursday-morning truffle market on Place Mistral in Aups, which has its own card.
avoid:Thinking the Var stops at the beac.why: Trade one beach day for an inland day, and build it round a market.
facts: A coast where nobody goes out of sight of the sea
Collobrières on Sunday 18 or 25 October 2026 for chestnuts (arrive before 9am); Aups on a Thursday morning from 26 November 2026 for truffles; the Verdon when the coast is hottest

avoid:Pale pink, and calling it terroir.name: Pale pink, and calling it terroir
avoid:Pale pink, and calling it terroir.teaser: Rosé made to photograph well in an ice bucket tells you nothing about where it grew
avoid:Pale pink, and calling it terroir.story: A great deal of Var rosé is made to a look: pale enough to photograph well in a beach-club ice bucket, and quiet about the ground it came from. Pale is a style, not a mark of quality. For a wine that tastes of a place, go to Bandol: reds built on Mourvèdre that must spend at least 18 months in wood and can keep for decades, and rosés with real grip, grown on terraced restanques above the sea. What a good Côtes de Provence rosé should taste like is on its own drink card.
avoid:Pale pink, and calling it terroir.why: Order a Bandol rosé instead of the house pink and notice how much more it holds its own with food.
facts: Ice buckets of very pale rosé, chosen for the colour
Taste at the Maison des Vins de Bandol at Le Castellet, or go to the Fête des Vins de Bandol on the port, 5-6 December 2026

follow:Var Tourisme.name: Var Tourisme
follow:Var Tourisme.teaser: The department's own tourism agency: the whole Var, from the Verdon and truffle country to the gulf
follow:Var Tourisme.story: Var Tourisme is the departmental tourism agency, based in Toulon and funded by the Conseil départemental; it sells the destination under the brand 'Le Var, L'Unique', and its Instagram is @levarlunique. It covers the whole territory rather than the beach-club coast, which makes it most useful out of season: inland villages, markets, the Verdon and the Haut-Var. Check it before planning a day away from the sea.
follow:Var Tourisme.why: Best for off-season and inland ideas, and the agenda of what is on.
facts: The Var's official departmental tourism agency

follow:Saint-Tropez Tourisme.name: Saint-Tropez Tourisme
follow:Saint-Tropez Tourisme.teaser: The town's tourist office: the Bravades, Les Voiles and the crowd and ferry news that times a visit
follow:Saint-Tropez Tourisme.story: Saint-Tropez's tourist office runs its own site and Instagram, @sainttropeztourisme. Follow it for the gulf's calendar, from the Bravades in May to Les Voiles in late September, and above all for the practical news that decides a day here: when the crowds peak, how the boats are running, what is open as the season winds down. The office itself is on the Allée du Quai de l'Épi by the port.
follow:Saint-Tropez Tourisme.why: Follow it for timing: when to come, how to get in, and what is still open in the shoulder months.

follow:Parc national de Port-Cros.name: Parc national de Port-Cros
follow:Parc national de Port-Cros.teaser: The custodian of Port-Cros and Porquerolles: the rules, the trails and what is in flower
follow:Parc national de Port-Cros.story: The national park manages Port-Cros, much of Porquerolles and the sea around them, and it posts what you need to know before you land: marine-reserve rules, trail closures, summer visitor limits and what is in bloom. On a protected island the rules are strict, so this is the account to read before a day ashore rather than after, and the place to look when the summer limits come back each year.
follow:Parc national de Port-Cros.why: Read it before you take a tender ashore: the rules on a national-park island are not suggestions.
facts: The national park authority for Port-Cros and Porquerolles

follow:Vins de Bandol.name: Vins de Bandol
follow:Vins de Bandol.teaser: The appellation's own voice: about 70 estates and three co-operatives across eight communes
follow:Vins de Bandol.story: The official body of the Bandol AOP speaks for some 70 estates and châteaux and three co-operatives across the appellation's eight communes. Follow it to learn where to taste the long-lived Mourvèdre reds and the rosés with grip, which estates open their doors and when, and for news of the Fête des Vins on the port of Bandol each December; this year it falls on 5 and 6 December 2026.
follow:Vins de Bandol.why: Use it to plan cellar visits, and to catch the December wine fair on the port.
facts: The official body of the Bandol appellation

follow:Villa Noailles.name: Villa Noailles
follow:Villa Noailles.teaser: The art centre above Hyères: Design Parade in June, the fashion and photography festival in October
follow:Villa Noailles.story: The Villa Noailles account is the pulse of the Var's design, fashion and photography scene, and the first place news appears about its two festivals: Design Parade, on interior design and objects, at the end of June (25-28 June in 2026), and the Festival International de Mode, Photographie et Accessoires in mid-October, which runs this week, 15-18 October 2026. The villa itself has its own card.
follow:Villa Noailles.why: Follow it from spring, when the festival programmes and the finalists are announced.
facts: The Villa Noailles art centre in Hyères and its festivals

follow:MICHELIN Guide France.name: MICHELIN Guide France
follow:MICHELIN Guide France.teaser: Where the stars are announced: the France & Monaco selection, revealed each spring
follow:MICHELIN Guide France.story: The MICHELIN Guide publishes its France & Monaco selection once a year at a televised ceremony. The 2026 edition was unveiled on 16 March 2026 at the Grimaldi Forum in Monaco, the first time the ceremony was held in the principality, with one new three-star restaurant, seven new two-stars and 54 new one-stars. Its site and app list every starred, Bib Gourmand and selected table in the Var, with inspectors' notes; the tables in this guide carry their own distinctions.
follow:MICHELIN Guide France.why: Watch it in early spring for the new stars; the 2027 ceremony date had not been announced when checked.

Hours conflict between listings for the Partégal mill; Cave de la Capte hours come from a 2021 listing; the Maison des Vins de Bandol listing was last updated Apr 2025; Maison des Vins Côtes de Provence summer hours unknown. Pampelonne's 'Tahiti' end is not in the plan documents found. Site fields: visitvar.fr, sainttropeztourisme.com and telepherique-faron.fr were confirmed by search; moulindupartegal.fr and cavedelacapte.com are named by listings; portcros-parcnational.fr, vinsdebandol.com, villanoailles.com and guide.michelin.com are given on prior knowledge (WebFetch unavailable to open them).
